lesson.title: Clocking a Reaction: What Average Rate Really Measures
lesson.summary: Average rate tells you how much a reactant's or product's concentration changes over a measurable stretch of time, giving the first practical handle on how fast a reaction runs.
lesson.body:
Before you can ask whether a reaction is fast or slow, you need a number to attach to that question. The reaction rate you have already met is defined as the change in concentration of a reactant or product divided by the time interval over which that change happens. When that interval is a real, measurable chunk of time, seconds, minutes, even hours, the quantity you calculate is called the average rate. It is the simplest, most direct way to quantify a reaction's speed because it only requires two measurements: a concentration at the start of the interval and a concentration at the end.

For a reactant A disappearing over time, the average rate is written as minus the change in [A] divided by the change in time, average rate = -delta[A]/delta t. The negative sign is not optional bookkeeping, it is there because [A] is decreasing (delta[A] is negative) while chemists define rate as a positive quantity. If you were tracking a product forming instead, you would drop the negative sign, since the product's concentration is increasing. On a graph of concentration versus time, which is exactly the kind of plot you built skills for when you worked with graphing data, the average rate over an interval is the slope of the straight line connecting the two endpoints, called a secant line.

Here is a worked example. Suppose a hypothetical reaction A leads to products, and a chemist measures [A] at three points in time: 1.00 M at t = 0 s, 0.81 M at t = 100 s, and 0.64 M at t = 200 s. The average rate over the first interval is average rate = -(0.81 M - 1.00 M)/(100 s - 0 s) = -(-0.19 M)/100 s = 0.19 M/100 s = 0.0019 M/s, or 1.9 x 10^-3 M/s. Over the second interval, average rate = -(0.64 M - 0.81 M)/(200 s - 100 s) = -(-0.17 M)/100 s = 0.17 M/100 s = 0.0017 M/s, or 1.7 x 10^-3 M/s.

Notice that the average rate is not the same in both intervals, it drops slightly as the reaction proceeds. That is not a mistake in the data, it is a real and common feature of reaction kinetics: as A gets used up, there is usually less of it available to react (fewer particles, fewer effective collisions), so the reaction tends to slow down. This single observation, that rate itself can change over the course of a reaction, is exactly why chemists eventually need a sharper tool than an interval average, a rate at one specific instant, which is the subject of the next chapter.
